wine.name: Ata Rangi Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, built in large part on the Abel clone, with Dijon clones planted beside it.
wine.sites: The house's oldest Pinot Noir plantings, the home block of 1980 among them, in vineyards close around the winery on the Martinborough Terrace: shallow silt loam over deep, free draining alluvial gravel.
wine.making: Fermented with indigenous yeasts, a share of the fruit as whole bunches and the rest destemmed, for some two to three weeks on skins. The malolactic fermentation is completed in oak, and the wine spends about eleven months in French oak barrels, around a third of them new, then rests for some months after blending before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and dried herb with a savoury edge; fine boned yet firm, with the concentration of small, thick skinned berries thinned by the wind, fresh acidity and a long, fine grained finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth with time, and the house's own retrospectives reach back through decades of vintages.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Built in large part on the Abel clone, Ata Rangi Pinot Noir comes from the house's oldest vines on the Martinborough Terrace, planted from 1980: dark cherry and dried herb, fine boned and firm. Pour it a little below room temperature in a wide glass.
records.story: In 1980 the founder bought a stony sheep paddock at the edge of Martinborough village and planted it, one of the first vineyards on a terrace that a soil survey of the late 1970s had likened to Burgundy. His first Pinot Noir cuttings came through a customs officer at Auckland. The story goes that the officer had seized a cutting smuggled into the country in a gumboot, said in the usual telling to come from Romanée-Conti, and propagated it; whatever its true source, the vine took the officer's name, Abel, and the Ata Rangi block became its mother planting, from which the clone spread across New Zealand. The founder's sister joined three years after the founding, and the first Ata Rangi Pinot Noir was released from the 1986 vintage, beside the first Célèbre, a red blend. In 1987 the founder married and his wife joined the family firm. The house added vineyards around the village over the following decades, among them a share of the Craighall vineyard, divided with Dry River in 2004. Its Pinot Noir came to stand for the district itself: savoury, firm, made from small crops thinned by the wind, and able to age.

wine.name: Dry River Pinot Gris
wine.grapes: Pinot Gris alone, from a small berried clone that the house traces to an import by the Mission in 1886.
wine.sites: The Dry River Estate vineyard on the Martinborough Terrace, most of the fruit from the first vines planted there in 1979, ungrafted by the house's account, in clay rich soil.
wine.making: The crop is kept very small and picked late. The fruit is fermented with its own yeasts, as is the house's rule across its whole range, and the wine is made with as little intervention as the house can manage, in its own words seeking to keep what the vineyard grew without embellishment.
wine.glass: Yellow peach, rock melon and a hint of old fashioned custard, with a savoury note of fenugreek; rich, full and textured, gently sweet in some vintages, soft in acidity, finishing dry with a trace of bitterness.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy on release, it is built, like the whole Dry River range, for long ageing, and reviewers of older vintages expect it to unfold over many years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting is needed, though an older bottle opens with a little air; a white wine glass of medium size.

records.table: Cropped very low and picked late from vines planted on the Martinborough Terrace in 1979, Dry River Pinot Gris gives yellow peach, melon and a rich, textured palate, and is made to age.
records.story: A couple founded Dry River in 1979, planting ungrafted Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Sauvignon Blanc on the Martinborough Terrace, among the first vines in the district. After a little wine in 1983, their first commercial vintage was 1984. From the start the house kept its crops very small, picked late and made wines for the cellar rather than for early drinking. After the volcanic eruptions of 1991 cooled the seasons, the founder laid a reflective white mulch under the vines to give the fruit more ultraviolet light, which can make up for a lack of heat, and as summers grew hotter the house took it up in 2014 and 2015. A part share in the Craighall vineyard, first planted in 1983, was bought in 1997, and in 2004 the rest of it was divided between Dry River and Ata Rangi. In 2003 the founders sold the estate to two American investors, and the founder stayed on as winemaker; in 2022 the family of one of them sold Dry River to a Wellington businessman, returning it to New Zealand hands. Through each change the Pinot Gris kept its place as the house's case for the grape: a white of weight and length from old vines on one estate, and proof that New Zealand Pinot Gris need not be a simple aromatic.

wine.name: Martinborough Vineyard Home Block Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the several clones of the Home Block.
wine.sites: The Home Block on the Martinborough Terrace, where the vineyard began in 1980, on free draining gravel; by the house's account its parts include the original block of the 10/5 clone, planted in 1980, and blocks of the Abel and UCD5 clones planted in 2002.
wine.making: The fruit is picked and sorted by hand and fermented with a small share of whole bunches that varies by vintage, about a tenth in some years. The wine is then aged for about twelve months in French oak barrels, a share of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and ripe plum over a savoury, earthy edge of forest floor; medium bodied and supple, with fresh acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth over the decade that follows in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius in a wide Burgundy glass; a young bottle can take half an hour in a carafe.

records.table: The block where Martinborough Vineyard began in 1980, by the house's account among the district's first Pinot Noir plantings, names its Home Block Pinot Noir: dark cherry and plum with a savoury edge, supple and fresh. Duck or mushrooms suit it.
records.story: In the late 1970s a government soil scientist studied the Wairarapa and reported that the climate and free draining soils around Martinborough resembled Burgundy's; the house dates the work to 1978, other accounts a year either side. In 1980 a group of partners, the soil scientist among them, founded Martinborough Vineyard on the terrace and planted the Home Block, and by the house's own account it was one of the first in the district to plant Pinot Noir and holds some of the oldest Pinot vines in New Zealand. A winemaker who joined in 1986 made the Pinot Noirs of the late 1980s and early 1990s that helped carry the district's name abroad. Its reserve Pinot Noir took the name Marie Zélie, after a French settler who had planted vines near Masterton in the 1880s, and a Home Block Pinot Noir appears by the vintage of 2013. In 2014 a listed New Zealand wine company made a full takeover offer for Martinborough Vineyard Estates, and the house passed into its hands. The Home Block keeps the estate's beginning in the glass: wine from the first vines, where Martinborough Pinot Noir began.

wine.name: Escarpment Kupe Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, all of it the Abel clone, by the house's account.
wine.sites: The home block on Te Muna Road, first planted in 1999, densely planted on alluvial gravel terraces at the edge of the Martinborough district.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters with indigenous yeasts, a share of the fruit as whole bunches that varies by vintage, from about a third to more than a half, hand plunged once a day for some four weeks on skins. The wine then spends eighteen to twenty months in French oak barriques, around two fifths to a half of them new, and is bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Black cherry, wild raspberry and fruit cake with clove and pepper; dense and peppery, tight when young, with firm, slightly leathery tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and somewhat closed on release, it wants several years in bottle and then holds for a decade or more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: Decant a young bottle for an hour; serve at 15 to 17 degrees Celsius in a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: All Abel clone and close planted, the home block on Te Muna Road gives Escarpment its Kupe Pinot Noir, made with a good share of whole bunches and long in French oak: black cherry, fruit cake and pepper, dense and firm. Decant it young.
records.story: The founder came to Martinborough in 1986 as winemaker of Martinborough Vineyard, and made its Pinot Noirs of the late 1980s and early 1990s. In late 1998 he and his wife, with Australian partners, bought land at 51 Te Muna Road, south east of the village, and in 1999 they planted the Escarpment vineyard as a joint venture, densely and with the Abel clone. By the house's own account Kupe began with the vintage of 2003, when a tiny crop from the low yielding home block was made into the single vineyard wine. Beside it the house made Pinot Noir from other single vineyards around the district, among them Kiwa and Pahi, and an Escarpment Pinot Noir under the house's name. In March 2018 Torbreck Vintners of the Barossa Valley announced that it would buy the business, and the purchase was completed in 2019 after the approval of New Zealand's Overseas Investment Office. Kupe, the house's flagship, is Martinborough Pinot Noir on its denser, more structured side: whole bunches and long barrel ageing from one close planted block.

wine.name: Palliser Estate Pinot Noir
wine.sites: Several of the house's vineyards on the Martinborough Terrace, drawn in large part from those it farms organically, Pencarrow among them.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is cold soaked and fermented largely with wild yeasts, a small share as whole bunches in some vintages. The wine is pressed to French oak barrels and matured for about ten months, during which the malolactic fermentation takes place, before bottling.
wine.glass: Black and red cherry, raspberry and mulberry with anise, dried herb and a note of freshly mown summer hay; silky and supple on the palate, savoury and structured.
wine.ageing: Ready within a couple of years of release, it keeps and gains savoury depth for several years after that.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with a little air; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Cape Palliser lends Palliser Estate its name, and its Pinot Noir comes mostly from organically farmed vineyards on the Martinborough Terrace: black cherry, raspberry and dried herb, silky and savoury. A Burgundy glass, a little cool, suits it.
records.story: Palliser takes its name from Cape Palliser, the headland at the southern end of the Wairarapa, which Captain James Cook (1728 to 1779) named after a British naval officer. The business began in 1984, when the Om Santi vineyard was planted on the Martinborough Terrace; a vineyard partnership followed in 1986, and in 1988 the two were joined in the company the house became. Its first wine came from the 1989 vintage. Unlike the family estates around it, Palliser was formed as an unlisted public company held by a small number of shareholders, and it made Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay beside its Pinot Noir. The vineyard then called Wharekauhau, planted in 1998, gave the house its first single vineyard wines and took the name Hua Nui after the 2018 vintage. Organic conversion began there in 2017, and in 2020 it became the first of the house's vineyards certified by BioGro. The Estate Pinot Noir, drawn mostly from those organic vineyards, is the house's bottle a guest is likeliest to meet: supple, savoury Martinborough Pinot Noir.

Pick doubt: the house's top Pinot Noir is the Single Vineyard Hua Nui; the Estate Pinot Noir is kept as the plan's pick, the wine a guest meets most.
The vineyard area, organic share and the claim to be the largest organic grower of the Wairarapa are volatile and left out.

changed: story, others and cards: Hua Nui first bottled on its own from 2018; now the vineyard called Wharekauhau, planted in 1998, gave the house's first single vineyard wines and took the name Hua Nui after the 2018 vintage, organic conversion from 2017 and BioGro certification in 2020 (Wine-Searcher, Fareham Wine Cellar, the house's sustainability page).

wine.sites: Hua Nui, Winery and Pencarrow said to give most of the fruit; now drawn in large part from the organically farmed vineyards, Pencarrow among them (a merchant's 2022 sheet), since Hua Nui is bottled alone.
wine.label, others and traps: Pencarrow mostly from the Pencarrow vineyard; now named for one vineyard and drawn from several that vary by vintage (Nick's, the New Zealand Wine Catalogue).
story: one of the larger houses of the district cut as a volatile size claim.
sources: Wine Anorak, a writer's own site, replaced by Wine-Searcher for the first harvest of 1989.
open: The planting years of Pencarrow (1998) and the Winery vineyard (2000) rest on the house's Our Land page alone and are no longer told.
